title: Agency & Partnership Practice Finals
description: 3 practice finals (90 questions), each 30 five-choice questions sized like the final's 60-minute multiple-choice part and running through the Weeks 1–14 outline in order: creating an agency, authority, ratification and estoppel, tort liability, agents' duties, partnership formation, property, management and duties, grabbing and leaving, dissolution under the UPA and RUPA, Kovacik, buyouts, LPs and LLPs, and the LLC weeks (formation, the operating agreement, veil piercing, fiduciary duties, capital and expulsion, and dissolution). Professor Richardson's format: stand-alone questions mixing rule questions ("Which of the following is NOT…") with short who-wins hypos, plus "None of the above," "All of the above" and combination choices. Every choice is explained. Use Exam mode to take a final under time and grade it, or Study mode to check each answer.
areas: Fiduciary Duties Between Agent and Principal

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT required to create an agency relationship?
o: An understanding that the principal will control the undertaking.
The agent's acceptance of the undertaking.
A contract supported by consideration.
The principal's manifestation that the agent will act on the principal's behalf.
None of the above; all of them are required.
oe: Required, though control can be minimal; the right to control, not its exercise, matters.
Required. The agent must manifest assent or otherwise consent to act.
Correct: this is not required. Agency rests on consent, not contract; a gratuitous agent is still an agent (Gorton v. Doty).
Required. It is the first of the three elements (R3d § 1.01; Botticello).
C is not required.

questions.q: Under A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, when does a creditor become the principal of its debtor?
o: Whenever it lends the debtor money.
Whenever it takes a security interest in the debtor's assets.
When it takes de facto control of the debtor's business.
Whenever it buys most of the debtor's products.
None of the above.
oe: Lending alone does not create agency (compare Martin v. Peyton).
Security interests are ordinary protections for a lender.
Correct. Cargill approved major decisions, audited, criticized daily, and supplied forms. A creditor that takes over management becomes a principal (R2d § 14O) and inherits the debtor's obligations.
A buyer is not a principal just because it buys most of the output (R2d § 14K).
C is correct.

questions.q: In Mill Street Church of Christ v. Hogan, Bill's authority to hire his brother Sam as a helper is best characterized as:
o: Express actual authority, because the elders hired Bill to do the job.
Apparent authority, because Sam reasonably believed Bill could hire him.
Implied actual authority, from past practice and the job's needs.
Inherent agency power arising from Bill's position.
None of the above; Bill lacked authority once the elders changed plans.
oe: The elders never told Bill to hire Sam.
The question was Bill's own reasonable understanding, which makes it actual authority.
Correct. Bill had been allowed to hire Sam before, and the job could not be done alone. The elders' secret change of plans did not control.
Unnecessary; actual authority existed.
Bill had implied actual authority, so Sam was the church's employee.

questions.q: Which of the following, standing alone, is NOT enough to give an agent apparent authority?
o: The principal's silence, when a reasonable person would object, while the agent claims authority in the principal's presence.
The principal's placing the agent in a position whose holders customarily have such authority.
The principal's letter to the third party naming the agent as its representative.
The principal's past payment of similar contracts the agent made with the same third party.
The agent's own statement to the third party that he is authorized.
oe: Silence where one would speak can be a manifestation (compare Ackerman, where the clients stood by during the settlement talks).
Position is a manifestation by the principal (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b; Kidd).
A direct written manifestation from the principal.
A prior course of dealing that the principal accepted is a manifestation to the third party.
Correct: this is not enough. Apparent authority must be traceable to the principal's manifestations to the third party; the agent's own say-so never suffices by itself (R3d § 3.03; Lind; Hoddeson).

questions.q: In Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, Inc., Judge Learned Hand held Edison bound to its contract with the singer because:
o: Fuller had express actual authority to hire the singer for a fully unconditional concert tour.
Hiring singers was within the customary scope of Fuller's job, and the limit was secret.
Edison later ratified the contract by accepting the singer's services.
The singer was Edison's employee rather than Fuller's.
None of the above.
oe: Fuller's secret instructions limited him to recitals dealers later booked.

Correct. Hiring singers without such an unusual condition was within the customary scope of Fuller's job, the limit was never communicated, and a principal who chooses an agent "vouches" for him. Third parties may rely on the customary scope of an agent's role.
Edison refused to pay.
Employment status was not the issue.
B is correct.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT required for a principal to ratify an agent's unauthorized act?
o: The principal knew, or had reason to know, the material facts.
The third party had not withdrawn from the transaction before the affirmance.
The act was done, or purported to be done, on the principal's behalf.
The principal affirms the entire transaction.
The principal communicated the affirmance to the third party in writing.
oe: Required. Ratification needs knowledge of all material facts (Ercanbrack; R3d § 4.06).
Required. Ratification is ineffective if the third party has already withdrawn (R3d § 4.05).
Required (R3d § 4.03; Botticello: the husband never claimed to act for his wife).
Required. There is no partial ratification (R3d § 4.07).
Correct: this is NOT required. Ratification may be express or implied, most commonly by knowingly accepting benefits, and even by silence where there is a duty to speak.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the requirements under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 228 for conduct to be within the scope of employment?
o: The conduct is of the kind the employee is employed to perform.
The conduct occurs substantially within the authorized time and space limits.
The conduct is actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the employer.
The employer expressly authorized the specific act.
If force is intentionally used, its use is not unexpectable by the employer.
oe: This is a § 228 requirement.
This is a § 228 requirement.
This is a § 228 requirement.
Correct: this is NOT required. Even forbidden acts can be within scope (R2d § 230).
This is a § 228 requirement.

questions.q: Gulfway Oil owns a service station and its equipment, sets the station's hours, pays most of its utilities, may end its arrangement with the operator at will, and may assign the operator "other duties" as it sees fit. Their contract calls the operator an independent "commission agent." A car left for service rolls out of the station and injures a pedestrian. Under Humble Oil & Refining Co. v. Martin, which of the following statements is true?
o: Gulfway is not liable, because the contract describes the operator as independent.
Gulfway is liable, because it had the right to control the station's daily operations.
Gulfway is not liable, because a supplier of branded fuel is never liable for a station's negligence.
Gulfway is liable only if it trained the operator negligently.
None of the above.
oe: Labels do not control; the right to control the station's operations does.

Correct. In Humble Oil & Refining Co. v. Martin, the oil company owned the station and products, set the hours, paid most utilities, could end the arrangement at will, and could assign other duties, which made the operator its servant despite the contract's label. Contrast Hoover v. Sun Oil, where the dealer set his own hours, hired his own staff, and bore his own profit and loss.
Liability depends on control; an oil company that keeps the right to control daily operations answers for them.
Vicarious liability for a servant's negligence does not depend on the master's own fault.
B is correct.

questions.q: Under the majority rule stated in Kerl v. Rasmussen, when is a franchisor vicariously liable for a franchisee's negligence?
o: Whenever the franchisee uses the franchisor's trademark.
When it controls the specific part of the operation that caused the harm.
Whenever the franchisor sets uniform quality standards.
Never, because a franchisee is always an independent business with its own owners.
None of the above.
oe: A trademark license alone does not make the franchisor a principal (Murphy v. Holiday Inns).
Correct. Quality and brand standards are not control. Arby's had no say over hiring or supervision, so it was not liable for the franchisee's negligent supervision.
System-wide quality standards protect the brand and are not control of daily operations.
Pervasive operational control can make a franchisor a principal (Parker v. Domino's; Miller v. McDonald's).
B is correct.

questions.area: Fiduciary Duties Between Agent and Principal
questions.tag: Customer lists as trade secrets (Town & Country)
questions.q: Kleen Team, a house-cleaning service, built its customer list through months of costly cold calls; the list is not public, and most households turned the company down. Three of its employees quit, form a competing service, and solicit only Kleen Team's customers, using names they remember from work. Under Town & Country House & Home Service v. Newbery, which of the following statements is true?
o: The former employees may solicit any customers they remember, because memory is not a trade secret.
Kleen Team may enjoin solicitation of its customers and recover damages.
The former employees may not open any competing cleaning service at all.
Kleen Team has no remedy, because the employees' duties ended when they quit.
None of the above.
oe: Town & Country protected a list developed through costly effort, even though the employees did not take a written copy.

Correct. In Town & Country, the court treated a customer list developed through costly cold calls as a trade secret, enjoined the former employees from soliciting those customers, and awarded damages, while leaving them free to compete for other business. Contrast Corroon & Black, where widely accessible lists of shoppers were not secret.
Without a non-compete, former employees may compete; they may not exploit the confidential list.
The duty not to use the former principal's trade secrets and confidential information survives the end of the agency.
B is correct.

questions.q: Vera leases a storefront to a bakery for rent equal to 8% of the bakery's net profits. Under RUPA § 202(c)(3), which of the following statements is true?
o: Vera is a partner only if she has also agreed to share losses.
Vera is a partner, because the bakery operates in a building she owns.
Vera is presumed to be a partner, because her payment varies with the bakery's profits.
Vera is presumed to be a partner, but she can rebut the presumption by showing that she never managed the bakery.
None of the above.
oe: Loss sharing is a factor, but the rent exception decides the presumption question here.
Co-ownership or ownership of property used by the business does not make a partnership.
A share received as rent is one of the listed exceptions.
Wrong. No presumption arises in the first place, because the profit share was received as rent (§ 202(c)(3)).

Correct. Profit sharing raises a presumption of partnership unless the profits were received in payment of rent, among other things (§ 202(c)(3)). Vera's share is rent, so no presumption arises, and nothing else suggests she co-owns the bakery.

questions.q: Martin v. Peyton held that the wealthy lenders were not partners of the brokerage firm primarily because:
o: They did not share in the firm's profits, only in a fixed return.
Their information and veto rights were reasonable protections for a large, risky loan.
They had no knowledge of the firm's business or its finances.
Their agreement expressly said they were not partners, and the court found that controlling.
None of the above.
oe: They did receive 40% of profits (capped), but as compensation for the loan.

Correct. Their information rights, veto over speculative deals, option to buy in, and escrowed resignations protected a large, risky loan; they could veto but not initiate transactions or bind the firm. Whether lenders cross into partnership is "a question of degree."
They had extensive information rights.
Labels do not control; the court examined the substance.
B is correct.

questions.q: Under UPA § 40(b), in what order are the liabilities of a partnership paid on liquidation?
o: Partners' capital, partners' loans, outside creditors, partners' profits.
Outside creditors, partners' loans, partners' capital, partners' profits.
Outside creditors, partners' capital, partners' loans, partners' profits.
Partners' loans, outside creditors, partners' capital, partners' profits.
None of the above.
oe: Outside creditors are always paid first.
Correct. That is the UPA § 40(b) order. (RUPA instead pays all creditors, including partner-creditors, together, then contributions, then surplus.)
Under the UPA, partner loans come before capital.
Outside creditors come first.
B is correct.

questions.q: Ann and Bo are equal partners in a RUPA window-washing partnership with no written agreement. Ann wants to hire a third washer; Bo says no. Ann hires one anyway, pays him $6,000 out of her own pocket, and asks the partnership to reimburse her. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Ann is not entitled to reimbursement, because one of two equal partners is not a majority and Bo never agreed to the hire.
Ann is entitled to reimbursement, because she spent the money for the partnership's benefit.
Ann is entitled to reimbursement, because each partner has equal rights in management and may make ordinary business decisions.
Ann is not entitled to reimbursement, because hiring employees is outside the ordinary course of a window-washing business.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In Summers v. Dooley, a partner who hired a worker over his equal partner's objection could not get reimbursement: business differences are decided by a majority, and one of two partners is not a majority. Compare National Biscuit v. Stroud, which protects outsiders, not a partner seeking reimbursement.
A partner is reimbursed for payments made in the course of partnership activities only if she complied with her duties in making them (RUPA § 401(b)); here the majority never approved the hire.
Equal management rights do not let one partner impose an expense over the other's objection, as between the partners themselves.
Hiring a worker is ordinary-course business; the problem is that no majority approved it.
A is correct.

questions.q: In Meinhard v. Salmon, what did Chief Judge Cardozo hold that Salmon owed Meinhard regarding the new lease?
o: Nothing, because the joint venture was about to end.
The entire new lease, because Meinhard had financed the original venture.
Damages for competing with the hotel during the lease term.
Disclosure of the opportunity, so Meinhard could compete for it.
None of the above.
oe: That was the dissent's view.
Meinhard received a half interest, not the whole lease.
The issue was the taken opportunity, not competition with the hotel.
Correct. As manager and co-venturer, Salmon owed "the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive." The deal was an extension of the venture, so Meinhard was entitled to share in it.
D is correct.

questions.q: In Meehan v. Shaughnessy, the departing partners had unfairly obtained client consents to move cases to their new firm. What did the court require?
o: The departing partners had to give up every client they had ever served.
No remedy, because partners may always leave and take clients.
They had to prove the clients would have come anyway, or hold those profits in trust.
The old firm had to prove the exact damages caused by each client's departure to the new firm.
None of the above.
oe: The remedy was tied to the cases whose consents were unfairly obtained.
Preparing to leave was permitted, but the way they solicited clients was not.

Correct. Because they breached loyalty in how they got the consents, the burden shifted to them to show the clients would have consented to removal in any event; otherwise they held the profits in constructive trust.
The court shifted the burden to the fiduciaries who breached.
C is correct.

questions.q: Under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), which of the following events results in a partner's dissociation?
o: The partner's death.
The partner's transfer of his entire transferable interest in the partnership.
The partner's expulsion in accordance with the partnership agreement.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True: death is a dissociation event (§ 601).
False. A transfer is not a dissociation; the transferor stays a partner. A transfer of the whole interest only gives the other partners a ground to expel him unanimously (§ 601(4)).
True: expulsion under the agreement is a dissociation event (§ 601(3)).
Correct. Death and expulsion under the agreement dissociate; a transfer of one's interest does not.
B is wrong: transferring a transferable interest is not dissociation.

questions.q: Under the UPA (1914), two companies form a partnership whose agreement calls it "permanent." One partner contributed licenses to its patents for the partnership's use. That partner then announces that it is ending the partnership. Under Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp., which of the following statements is true?
o: The dissolution is wrongful, and the innocent partner may continue the business using the patents.
The patent-contributing partner may take back its patents immediately, because they remain its property.
The dissolution is rightful, because a partner always has the right to end a partnership.
The dissolution is wrongful, so the partnership must be liquidated and the patents sold at auction.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under UPA § 38(2), after a wrongful dissolution the innocent partners may continue the business, use the partnership property, and pay the wrongdoer the value of its interest, excluding goodwill and less damages. Pav-Saver applied this to the contributed patents.
In Pav-Saver the court let the innocent partner continue the business and keep using the patents.
A partner always has the power to dissolve, but not always the right; ending a "permanent" partnership breaches the agreement.
Wrongful dissolution gives the innocent partner the option to continue, not just a liquidation.
A is correct.

questions.q: Under Kovacik v. Reed, when one partner contributes all of the money and the other contributes only services, and the venture loses the capital, what happens?
o: The service partner must pay the money partner half of the lost capital.
Losses are shared in proportion to each partner's capital contribution.
Each partner loses their own contribution, money or labor.
The money partner may recover all of the lost capital from the service partner.
None of the above.
oe: That is the statutory result under UPA § 18(a), which Kovacik declined to apply.
Kovacik did not adopt a capital-ratio rule; the service partner contributed no capital.
Correct. The court held that the party who contributed money may not recover any part of it from the party who contributed only services.
Nothing supports making the service partner bear all of the money loss.
C is correct.

questions.q: A partnership agreement provides that either partner may name a price, and the other partner must then either buy the first partner's interest at that price or sell his own interest at that price. Which of the following statements best describes this clause?
o: The offering partner has a reason to name a fair price, since the other may buy at it.
The clause is unenforceable, because the RUPA requires an Article 7 buyout at going-concern value.
The partner who receives the offer must sell at the named price.
The price is set by a court-appointed appraiser if the partners disagree.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The first mover sets the price, but the other side chooses whether to buy or sell at it, so naming a low price risks having to sell cheap, and naming a high price risks having to buy dear.
The § 701 buyout rules are defaults the partners may replace by agreement.
The recipient chooses to buy or to sell; that choice is what disciplines the price.
This clause avoids appraisal; the named price controls.
A is correct.

questions.q: Rosa and Theo agree to open a bike shop. Rosa will invest $50,000 and stay out of daily operations; Theo will run the shop. They sign a written agreement calling Rosa a "limited partner" and Theo the "general partner," but they never file a certificate of limited partnership. The shop later defaults on a $90,000 supplier contract. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Rosa may be treated as a general partner and held personally liable for the shop's debts.
Rosa is not liable, because she took no part in running the shop.
Rosa is liable only up to her $50,000 investment, because the written agreement makes her a limited partner.
Rosa is liable only if the supplier knew she had invested in the shop.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. With no certificate on file, no LP was formed. Rosa and Theo are co-owners carrying on a business for profit, which is a general partnership whatever they called themselves (RUPA § 202(a)), and general partners are personally liable for partnership obligations (§ 306(a)).
Staying out of management is what a limited partner does, but Rosa never became one. Without a filed certificate, two co-owners running a business for profit are general partners.
A limited partnership exists only once a certificate is filed with the state. A private agreement cannot give Rosa a limited partner's shield against outsiders.
Partners' liability for partnership obligations comes from their status, not from the creditor's knowledge of who they are.
A is correct.

questions.tag: Agent who never identifies the LLC
questions.q: Rafe and Lena are the managers and members of Cobalt Ridge Holdings, LLC, whose articles are on file with the state. Rafe hires Tern Surveying to stake out a building lot. He hands Tern a card reading only "CRH" with an address, says he is "working on this for the group," and never mentions an LLC. Tern does the work and is not paid. Under Water, Waste & Land v. Lanham, is Rafe personally liable?
o: No, because the filed articles gave Tern constructive notice that it was dealing with an LLC.
No, because a manager is never liable for an LLC's debts solely by reason of being a manager.
No, because Tern knew Rafe was acting for some group rather than for himself.
Yes, because every member of an LLC guarantees the contracts its managers sign.
Yes, because he acted for a principal whose identity Tern was never told.
oe: Water, Waste & Land read the notice statute narrowly: filed articles give notice of LLC status only once the company is identified, and they do not displace agency law when the agent never named the company.
That is the status-based shield (RULLCA § 304(a)), but Tern sues Rafe as an agent, not as a manager; agency law makes an agent for an unidentified principal a party to the contract.
Knowing that an agent acts for someone is not enough. The principal was only partially disclosed, and the agent of a partially disclosed principal is liable.
Members do not guarantee company contracts; the shield of RULLCA § 304(a) protects them unless they agree otherwise.

Correct. An agent avoids liability only by disclosing both that he acts for a principal and who the principal is. "CRH" and "the group" disclosed a principal but not its identity, so Rafe is a party to the contract (Water, Waste & Land).
questions.e: An LLC's agent who discloses a principal but not its identity is a party to the contract; a statute making filed articles notice of LLC status protects only against status-based liability (Water, Waste & Land; RULLCA § 304(a)).

questions.q: Under the RULLCA, in a manager-managed LLC, which of the following requires the consent of all members?
o: An act outside the ordinary course of the LLC's activities.
Amending the operating agreement.
An ordinary hiring decision.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True.
True.
False. Ordinary matters are decided by the managers.
Correct. As in a member-managed LLC, acts outside the ordinary course and amendments to the operating agreement need unanimous member consent.
C is wrong.

questions.tag: LLC agreement binds the LLC; forum clause covers derivative claims
questions.q: Harbin Corp. and Dov form Quill Coatings, LLC under Delaware law. Their LLC agreement, which the LLC itself never signs, requires that any dispute arising out of the agreement or the manager's conduct be arbitrated in Oregon. Harbin later sues Dov, the manager, in the Delaware Court of Chancery, alleging that he looted the company, and labels its claims derivative, brought on the LLC's behalf. What is the most likely result?
o: The suit proceeds, because the LLC never signed the agreement and its claims are not bound.
The suit proceeds, because the Delaware Act gives Chancery jurisdiction over derivative claims.
The suit proceeds, because a fiduciary-duty claim can never be sent to arbitration by agreement.
The suit is dismissed only as to Harbin's direct claims; the derivative claims stay in Delaware.
The suit is dismissed, because the members agreed to arbitrate such claims in Oregon.
oe: Elf Atochem North America held that the LLC agreement binds the LLC even though the LLC did not sign it.
The Act's grants of jurisdiction (§§ 18-110(a), 18-111, 18-1001) are defaults; members may contract around them to choose another forum (Elf Atochem North America).
Delaware favors arbitration, and Elf Atochem North America sent fiduciary-duty claims against the manager to arbitration under the agreement.
Elf Atochem North America refused to treat derivative claims differently; the clause covered every claim arising out of the agreement or the manager's conduct.

Correct. Under Delaware's freedom-of-contract policy (DLLCA § 18-1101(b)), the agreement binds the LLC and its members, and its forum and arbitration clauses cover claims whether framed as direct or derivative (Elf Atochem North America).
questions.e: The LLC agreement binds the LLC though it did not sign it, and members may validly agree to arbitrate or litigate elsewhere all claims, direct or derivative (Elf Atochem North America; DLLCA § 18-1101(b)).

questions.q: Ines is the sole member of Vantage Air Partners, LLC, a Delaware LLC that leases a share of a private jet from Altair Jets. Ines and her family fly the LLC's hours on vacations, she moves money in and out of the LLC's account whenever she likes, and her deposits are booked as "loans" so she can withdraw them at will. The LLC stops paying and has no assets. Altair sues Ines personally. Under NetJets Aviation v. LHC Communications, what is the most likely result?
o: Altair can reach Ines by proving a single economic entity and an element of injustice.
Ines wins, because Altair cannot prove she committed actual fraud in signing the lease.
Altair can reach Ines if it shows she ignored formal meetings and kept no minutes.
Ines wins, because an LLC's sole member is never liable for the LLC's contract debts.
Altair wins automatically, because a single-member LLC has no separate existence.
oe: Correct. Delaware's test asks (1) whether the LLC and its owner operated as a single economic entity and (2) whether there was an overall element of injustice or unfairness. Treating the account as her own pocket and disguising withdrawals as loan repayments could satisfy both (NetJets Aviation).
Delaware does not require actual fraud; an overall element of injustice or unfairness is enough when combined with a single economic entity (NetJets Aviation).

Missing internal formalities count for less with an LLC, which needs few of them; RULLCA § 304(b) even says that ignoring formalities is not a ground for liability. Siphoning and commingling are what matter.
Piercing is an exception to the shield; Delaware applies its corporate alter-ego doctrine to LLCs (NetJets Aviation).
A single-member LLC is a separate entity (RULLCA § 108(a)); piercing requires proof, and NetJets Aviation only sent the claim to trial.
questions.e: To pierce a Delaware LLC: (1) the LLC and owner operated as a single economic entity, and (2) an overall element of injustice or unfairness; fraud is not required (NetJets Aviation).

questions.tag: Secret written consent to strip the majority's protection
questions.q: Juno owns 60% of Starfield, LLC, a Delaware LLC managed by a three-person board, and the agreement lets her appoint and remove two of the three managers. Her appointee, Cal, secretly sides with the third manager, Dax. Without telling Juno, Cal and Dax sign a written consent merging Starfield into a corporation in which Dax's side holds the majority. The LLC Act permits managers to act by written consent without prior notice. Under VGS v. Castiel, is the merger valid?
o: Yes, because a majority of the board acted, which the agreement and the statute allow.
Yes, because the managers owed no duty to give notice before acting by written consent.
No, because Delaware requires the board of a manager-managed LLC to act unanimously on a merger.
No, because acting in secret to defeat Juno's protection breached their duty of loyalty.
Yes, but Juno may recover damages from Cal for disobeying the manager who appointed him.
oe: VGS agreed that the board could act by majority, but technically authorized action can still be inequitable.
The statute, read literally, required no notice, but the court held that using written consent to prevent the majority owner from protecting itself breached the duty of loyalty.
VGS held the opposite on this point: the agreement implied majority action by the board, not unanimity.

Correct. The managers knew notice would let Juno remove Cal and block the plan; acting clandestinely to strip the majority of its bargained-for protection breached their duty of loyalty, so the merger was invalid and rescinded (VGS; DLLCA § 18-404(d)).
The court did not treat the case as one for damages against Cal; it invalidated the merger itself.
questions.e: Managers who use a statutory shortcut (written consent without notice) to defeat the majority owner's bargained-for protection breach their duty of loyalty; the action is invalid (VGS).

questions.tag: Manager-managed LLC: who owes the duties (§ 409(i))
questions.q: Under RULLCA, in a manager-managed LLC, which of the following statements is NOT correct?
o: The managers owe the company the duties of loyalty and care.
A member owes no duty to the company solely by reason of being a member.
Each member must refrain from competing with the company until the company dissolves.
A manager's duty not to compete with the company lasts until winding up is completed.
Both the managers and the members must act consistently with good faith and fair dealing.
oe: Correctly stated. In a manager-managed LLC the loyalty and care duties of § 409(b) and (c) apply to the managers (§ 409(i)(1)).
Correctly stated (§ 409(i)(6)).

This is the incorrect statement, so it is the answer. In a manager-managed LLC the noncompete and other § 409(b) duties apply to the managers, not the members (§ 409(i)(1)); the member-managed rule is the one tied to dissolution.
Correctly stated. For managers, the noncompete continues until winding up is completed (§ 409(i)(2)).
Correctly stated. The obligation of good faith and fair dealing binds managers and members alike (§ 409(i)(3)).
questions.e: In a manager-managed LLC, the managers owe loyalty and care (with the noncompete lasting through winding up), members owe no duty merely as members, and everyone owes good faith and fair dealing (RULLCA § 409(i)).

questions.tag: Capital-call clause is not a guaranty of LLC debts
questions.q: Bluegrass Stables, LLC's operating agreement obliges its investor members to contribute, in proportion to their interests, whatever amounts the manager reasonably deems advisable to pay the company's expenses. The LLC, now defunct, owes a feed supplier a $60,000 judgment. The supplier asks the court to order the manager to make a final capital call so the members will pay the judgment. Under Racing Investment Fund 2000 v. Clay Ward Agency, how should the court rule?
o: Order the call, because the feed was a business expense the clause covers.
Order the call, but limit each member to his pro rata share of the judgment.
Refuse, because only the members, not the LLC's creditors, may enforce the clause.
Refuse; the clause is not a clear agreement to answer for the LLC's debts.
Refuse, unless the supplier first shows grounds to pierce the LLC's veil.
oe: The expense may be one the manager could have called capital for, but that does not turn a funding clause into a debt-collection device a court can use against the members.
Pro rata or not, ordering the call would impose personal liability for the LLC's debt, which the members never clearly agreed to.
This misstates the reason. The court did not rest on who may enforce the clause; it held that the clause was not an agreement to answer for the LLC's debts.

Correct. Members are not liable for an LLC's debts unless they agree in writing to be, and because that defeats the point of an LLC, the agreement must be unequivocal. An ordinary capital-infusion clause does not qualify (Racing Investment Fund 2000; compare RULLCA § 304(a)).
Veil piercing is a separate theory the supplier did not raise; the court decided that the capital-call clause itself creates no member liability.
questions.e: A clause letting a manager call for capital to pay expenses is not a member's agreement to be personally liable for LLC debts; that assumption must be stated unequivocally (Racing Investment Fund 2000).

questions.q: Under the RULLCA, which of the following does NOT cause an LLC to dissolve?
o: An event the operating agreement says causes dissolution.
The consent of all the members.
A court order on a member's application, for example because the LLC's business is unlawful.
The passage of 90 consecutive days during which the LLC has no members.
A member's dissociation.
oe: A dissolution event (§ 701).
A dissolution event (§ 701).
A dissolution event (§ 701).
A dissolution event (§ 701).
Correct: this does not dissolve the LLC. A member's dissociation leaves the LLC in place; the dissociated member holds her interest as a transferee (§ 603).

questions.tag: Deadlock; exit clause leaves the member on a guaranty
questions.q: Kit and Rowan each own 50% of a Delaware LLC whose only asset is the land under a restaurant. They no longer speak, and every LLC decision needs both of them. Their agreement lets a member who quits be bought out at fair market value by the other, but it would not release Kit from his personal guaranty of the LLC's mortgage. Kit petitions for judicial dissolution, and Rowan argues that Kit must use the exit clause instead. Under Haley v. Talcott, what is the most likely result?
o: Dissolution is ordered, since the exit clause leaves Kit liable on the guaranty.
Dissolution is denied, because the agreement supplies an exclusive exit mechanism.
Dissolution is denied, because the LLC still collects rent and pays its mortgage.
Dissolution is ordered, because any deadlock between members requires it.
Dissolution is denied, because only the LLC's manager may petition for it.
oe: Correct. Applying DGCL § 273 by analogy (two 50% owners, a joint venture, and no agreement on the future), the court found it not reasonably practicable to continue under DLLCA § 18-802, and it would be inequitable to force Kit to exit while he stayed on the guaranty (Haley).
An exit clause defeats dissolution only if it is an adequate, equitable alternative; this one was not, and nothing made it exclusive.
Haley dissolved an LLC that was "technically functioning"; the question is whether it is reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with the agreement, not whether it is solvent.
Deadlock is a strong factor, but dissolution remains discretionary and the court weighs any contractual exit; Haley turned on the inadequate exit clause.
Section 18-802 allows an application by or for a member or manager.
questions.e: A Delaware court may dissolve a deadlocked 50/50 LLC under § 18-802 when it is not reasonably practicable to continue, unless the agreement offers an adequate and equitable exit (Haley).

questions.q: In Gorton v. Doty, the court held that the coach who drove the teacher's car to the football game was the teacher's agent, even though:
o: The coach was not paid.
There was no written agreement between them.
The teacher did not direct how the coach drove the car.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Consideration and payment are not required for agency; a gratuitous agent is still an agent.
True. Agency rests on consent, not on a contract or writing.
True. Control can be minimal: naming the driver was enough. The right to control, not its actual exercise, matters.
Incomplete. C is also true.
Correct. A gratuitous favor with one condition (only the coach may drive) supplied consent and control. No pay, no contract, and no detailed control were needed.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of a special agent rather than a general agent?
o: A store manager who runs a shop's daily operations for its owner.
A purchasing director who buys supplies for a hotel chain year after year.
A real estate broker hired to sell one particular house.
A resident manager who collects rents and arranges repairs for an apartment building.
None of the above.
oe: A store manager conducts a continuous series of transactions, which makes her a general agent.
Ongoing purchasing is a continuous series of transactions, so this is a general agent.
Correct. A special agent is authorized to conduct a single transaction or a series of transactions not involving continuity of service (R2d § 3). A broker hired for one sale fits.
Managing a building over time is a continuous series of transactions, which makes this a general agent.
C is correct.

questions.q: Harmon Paper Co. makes Lucia its regional sales manager, a post whose holders in the paper industry customarily grant volume discounts of up to 15%. Harmon's president privately tells Lucia not to grant any discount above 5%. Lucia grants a long-time customer, Crestview Printing, a 12% discount. Crestview knows nothing of the 5% cap. Is Harmon bound to the 12% discount?
o: Yes, because by placing Lucia in a position whose holders customarily grant such discounts, Harmon manifested that she had that authority.
No, because Lucia told Crestview nothing about her authority.
Yes, but only if Harmon later ratifies the discount.
No, because Lucia lacked actual authority to grant more than 5%.
Yes, because a sales agent always has the power to bind her principal to whatever discount she grants, whatever the custom of the trade and whatever the principal has privately told her.
oe: Correct. A principal that puts an agent in a position makes a manifestation that the agent has the authority customarily held there, and a third party need not inquire into undisclosed limits (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b; Lind v. Schenley).
Apparent authority does not depend on the agent's statements. It comes from the principal's manifestation, and placing an agent in a position is such a manifestation.
Ratification is another route, but Harmon is already bound without it.
Lack of actual authority is only the first step. Harmon can still be bound through apparent authority.
Too broad. The authority reaches what is customary for the position; a discount far outside custom would not be reasonably believed.

questions.tag: Told not to hire, but custom allows
questions.q: Ann manages an apartment building for its owner, Paul. Paul tells her, "Do not hire a janitor." Resident managers customarily hire janitors, and Ann hires one from CleanCo, which knows nothing of Paul's instruction. Which of the following statements is true?
o: No actual authority, but Paul may be bound if CleanCo reasonably relied on Ann's position.
Ann had implied actual authority, because local custom allows resident managers to hire janitors.
Paul cannot be bound, because Ann disobeyed a direct order.
Ann had express authority, because she was hired to manage the building.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The casebook's apartment-manager hypo: Paul's express instruction controls between Paul and Ann, so there is no actual authority. But placing Ann in a role that customarily carries this power is a manifestation to third parties, who need not inquire about secret limits (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b).
Custom can supply implied authority only when the principal has not said otherwise. An express instruction controls.
Disobedience ends actual authority, not necessarily apparent authority.
Express authority covers what the principal actually said, and Paul said the opposite.
A is correct.

questions.q: Ivo, a wine buyer, orders $30,000 of wine from Cask & Barrel, telling the seller he is buying "for a restaurant group I represent, which prefers to stay anonymous." The wine is delivered, and no one pays. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Only the restaurant group is liable, because Cask & Barrel knew Ivo was acting as an agent.
Ivo is a party to the contract, because the seller never learned who his principal was.
Only Ivo is liable, because a principal whose identity is not disclosed can never be bound.
No one is liable, because Cask & Barrel agreed to sell without knowing who the buyer was.
None of the above.
oe: Knowing that an agent is acting for someone is not enough to release the agent. The seller did not know who the principal was.

Correct. When the third party knows the agent acts for a principal but does not know the principal's identity, the principal is unidentified (partially disclosed), and the agent is a party to the contract unless the parties agree otherwise (R3d § 6.02; Atlantic Salmon A/S v. Curran).
An unidentified principal that authorized the deal is bound once identified.
Choosing to deal with an anonymous principal through an agent is exactly why the law makes the agent a party.
B is correct.

questions.q: Under Hoddeson v. Koos Bros., what must a customer who paid an impostor posing as a salesman prove to hold the store liable by estoppel?
o: The store failed to use reasonable care to keep impostors from appearing to be its staff.
The customer reasonably relied on the appearance of authority.
The customer changed position to her detriment, as by paying the money.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Required.
Required.
Required.
Incomplete. Detrimental change of position is also required.
Correct. There was no apparent authority, because the store made no manifestation, but estoppel can rest on the store's carelessness plus the customer's reliance and change of position.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 220(2) in deciding whether a worker is a servant?
o: Whether the worker has ever been sued for negligence.
Whether the employer or the worker supplies the tools and the place of work.
Whether the worker is paid by the hour or by the job.
Whether the work is part of the employer's regular business.
The extent of control the employer may exercise over the details of the work.
oe: Correct: NOT a factor. The others also include skill, a distinct occupation, length of employment, the parties' belief, and whether the principal is in business.
A § 220 factor.
A § 220 factor.
A § 220 factor.
A § 220 factor.

questions.q: Lyle drives a tow truck for Ace Towing, whose rules forbid drivers to help stranded motorists except on dispatched calls. On his way back to the yard, Lyle stops to push a stranger's stalled car for a $20 tip, and the push causes a collision. The injured driver sues Ace. Under Brill v. Davajon, which of the following statements is true?
o: Ace is liable, because Lyle was driving Ace's truck during working hours.
Ace is liable, because forbidden acts are always within the scope of employment.
Ace is not liable; the push was outside the scope of employment.
Ace is not liable, because tow-truck drivers are independent contractors.
None of the above.
oe: Using the employer's vehicle during work hours does not make every act within scope; the purpose of the act matters.
Forbidden acts can be within scope (R2d § 230), but not when the employee departs from the employer's business to serve only himself.

Correct. In Brill v. Davajon, a cab driver who pushed a stalled car for $1, against company rules, was outside the scope of employment: the act served only his own purpose (R2d § 228(1)(c)). Contrast Bushey's enterprise-risk view.
Nothing suggests Lyle is an independent contractor; the issue is scope of employment.
C is correct.

questions.q: In Anderson v. Marathon Petroleum Co., Marathon was not liable for the death of the contractor's employee from silicosis because:
o: Sandblasting with proper equipment is not an abnormally dangerous activity.
The contractor's own employees are covered by workers' compensation, which the principal already pays for through the contract price.
Marathon did not know about the inadequate hood.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True.
True. This is Posner's explanation of why the contractor's own workers are treated differently from neighbors.
False. Marathon knew and did nothing.
Correct.
C is false.

questions.area: Fiduciary Duties Between Agent and Principal
questions.q: While still employed as the sales manager of Delta Tools, Ned plans to start a competing business. Which of the following is Ned permitted to do before he leaves?
o: Form an LLC for the new business and open its bank account.
Persuade Delta's top salespeople to quit and join his new business.
Sign a lease for office space for the new business.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Preparing to compete, such as forming an entity, is permitted if not otherwise wrongful (R3d § 8.04).
False. Using his position to recruit the principal's key employees while still employed is a breach (Bancroft-Whitney v. Glen).
True. Lining up space and financing is permitted preparation.
Correct. Forming the entity and leasing space are permitted preparations; soliciting Delta's employees while still its manager is not.
B is a breach of the duty of loyalty.

questions.q: Under RUPA § 202(c)(3), a person who receives a share of a business's profits is presumed to be a partner unless the profits were received in one of several excepted capacities. Which of the following recipients would be presumed to be a partner?
o: A seller of equipment who is being paid the purchase price in installments equal to 5% of profits.
A store manager who receives 10% of profits as a bonus on top of a salary.
A landlord who receives 8% of the tenant's profits as rent.
The widow of a deceased partner who receives 3% of profits as a retirement annuity.
None of the above.
oe: Excepted: profits received in payment of a debt by installments or otherwise.
Excepted: profits received as wages or other compensation to an employee.
Excepted: profits received as rent.
Excepted: profits received as an annuity or other retirement or health benefit to a beneficiary or representative of a deceased or retired partner.

Correct. Each recipient falls within an exception to the presumption: debt repayment, wages, rent, and an annuity to a deceased partner's widow. (The other exceptions are interest on a loan, even if it varies with profits, and the price of goodwill or other property.)

questions.q: Why did the court in Young v. Jones reject partnership by estoppel against the U.S. Price Waterhouse firm?
o: Because the two firms were in different countries.
Because partnership by estoppel has been abolished.
No one relied on any representation of partnership.
Because the U.S. firm had filed a statement denying partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Geography was not the reason.
It survives in UPA § 16 and RUPA § 308.
Correct. Worldwide-firm advertising was not enough without reliance by these plaintiffs.
No such statement was the basis of the holding.
C is correct.

questions.q: Lars's personal creditor, not a creditor of the partnership, wins a judgment against him and obtains a charging order against his transferable interest in a RUPA partnership. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The creditor becomes a partner in Lars's place.
Lars is automatically dissociated.
The creditor gets Lars's distributions, but no role in management.
The creditor may seize partnership equipment to satisfy the judgment.
None of the above.
oe: At most, the creditor (or a buyer at foreclosure) becomes a transferee, not a partner.
A charging order is not a dissociation event.

Correct. A charging order is a lien on the judgment debtor's transferable interest that requires the partnership to pay the creditor any distribution owed to the debtor (§ 504). It gives no management or information rights.
Partnership property belongs to the entity, not to Lars, and his personal creditors cannot reach it directly.
C is correct.

questions.q: In a two-partner firm, partner X tells a supplier in advance that X objects to a routine purchase. Partner Y makes the purchase anyway. Reading National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud with Summers v. Dooley, which statement is most accurate?
o: The partnership is not bound, because X's objection was communicated to the supplier.
The partnership is bound, and Y may always make the partnership reimburse the cost, because the purchase was in the ordinary course.
Neither the partnership nor Y is bound, because the partners are deadlocked.
The partnership is bound to the supplier, but as between the partners, Y acted without majority approval.
None of the above.
oe: In National Biscuit, Stroud's notice did not help him: as one of two equal partners he was not a majority and could not restrict Freeman.
Summers v. Dooley denied reimbursement for an expense the majority never approved.
Deadlock suspends the power to act internally, but it does not void transactions with third parties.

Correct. As to third parties National Biscuit controls; among the partners Summers controls. The two cases fit together: a partner with apparent authority binds the firm to an outsider, while a split between equal partners leaves no majority for the expense internally.
D is correct.

questions.q: Under RUPA § 409(b)(3), a partner's duty to refrain from competing with the partnership:
o: Applies before the partnership dissolves.
Applies only if the partnership agreement contains a non-compete clause.
Continues for the rest of the partner's life.
Applies only to the managing partner.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The statute requires a partner to refrain from competing with the partnership in the conduct of its business before its dissolution. Other loyalty duties, such as accounting for benefits derived in winding up, continue during winding up (Monin v. Monin).
It is a statutory default that applies without any clause.
The no-compete duty is tied to the life of the partnership.
Every partner owes it.
A is correct.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is consistent with Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray and Bohatch v. Butler & Binion?
o: Partners may expel a partner under a negotiated no-cause expulsion clause, in good faith, as long as nothing owed to the expelled partner is wrongfully withheld.
Partners owe no fiduciary duty not to expel a partner for reporting suspected overbilling by another partner.
Expelling a partner always breaches the duty of loyalty.
None of the above.
A and B.
oe: Consistent with Lawlis.
Consistent with Bohatch.
Inconsistent with both cases.
A and B are consistent.
Correct. Courts enforce "guillotine" expulsion clauses as written, and partners may part ways when trust breaks down.

questions.q: Under the UPA (1914), which of the following is true of a partner's power to dissolve a partnership for a definite term before the term ends?
o: The partner has neither the power nor the right to dissolve before the term ends.
The partner has the power to dissolve, but using it early is wrongful.
The partnership agreement can eliminate the partner's power to dissolve.
The partner has the right to dissolve whenever the partnership is losing money.
None of the above.
oe: Under the UPA a partner always has the power to dissolve.
Correct. Power, not always the right: premature dissolution is wrongful but still occurs (Collins v. Lewis).
The power cannot be contracted away.
Losses alone do not give a right to dissolve, especially losses caused by the partner (Collins).
B is correct.

questions.q: In a RUPA partnership at will, a partner gives notice of their express will to withdraw. What is the result?
o: Dissociation only; the others continue and buy out the partner under Article 7.
Nothing happens until a court approves the withdrawal.
The partnership is dissolved and its business must be wound up (§ 801(1)).
A wrongful dissociation that makes the partner liable for damages.
None of the above.
oe: In an at-will partnership, express will to withdraw is a § 801(1) dissolution event, so the § 603 switch goes to Article 8.
No court approval is needed.

Correct. In an at-will partnership a partner's express will to withdraw causes both dissociation and dissolution. (The partners may still agree to continue the business, but the default is winding up.)
Withdrawal from an at-will partnership is rightful unless it breaches an express term.
C is correct.

questions.q: Nina and Owen form a UPA partnership to restore antique furniture, agreeing to split profits equally and saying nothing about losses. Nina contributes $40,000. Owen contributes $500 and all of the restoration work. The business fails, and $20,000 of Nina's capital is lost. In a jurisdiction that follows Kovacik v. Reed, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Owen owes Nina nothing, because Owen contributed his labor, and a partner who contributes services is never liable for capital losses.
Owen must share the capital loss with Nina as the statute provides, because he made a capital contribution.
Owen owes Nina nothing, because they never agreed to share losses.
Owen must repay all of Nina's lost capital, because he controlled the restoration work that caused the losses.
None of the above.
oe: The Kovacik rule applies only to a partner who contributed services alone. Owen contributed some capital, so the exception does not fit.

Correct. Kovacik is a narrow exception to UPA § 18(a), and courts do not apply it when the service partner made any capital contribution, even a nominal one, or was paid a salary. The statute's rule applies: losses are shared like profits.
Silence on losses brings in the default rule that losses are shared like profits (UPA § 18(a)); Kovacik is the only exception, and it does not apply here.
No rule makes the managing partner bear all losses; losses are shared like profits.
B is correct.

questions.tag: Suing for dissolution doesn't dissolve (G & S)
questions.q: A partnership agreement lets the surviving partners continue the business and buy a deceased partner's interest by formula. One partner, Yale, files suit asking a court to dissolve the partnership. Before the case is decided, Yale dies. His estate argues that his lawsuit dissolved the partnership, so the buyout clause does not apply. Under G & S Investments v. Belman, which of the following statements is true?
o: The estate is right, because filing a suit for dissolution dissolves a partnership on the day the suit is filed.
The estate is wrong; filing suit did not dissolve the partnership, so the buyout clause governs.
The estate is right, because a partner's death always dissolves the partnership whatever the agreement says.
The estate is wrong, but only because Yale's lawsuit was frivolous.
None of the above.
oe: G & S held that filing suit did not dissolve the partnership.
Correct. In G & S Investments v. Belman, the partner's suit for dissolution did not itself dissolve the partnership; when he died, the agreement's continuation and buyout provisions applied.
Partners may agree that the business continues after a death; the court enforced that agreement.
The merits of Yale's lawsuit were not the basis of the holding; filing it simply did not dissolve the firm.
B is correct.

questions.q: Hal and Ivy are limited partners in Westgate Storage, L.P., and also the officers of Westgate GP, Inc., its only general partner. Acting as officers of the corporation, they sign a supply contract that the LP later breaches. The supplier knew it was dealing with a limited partnership whose general partner was a corporation. Under Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, Inc., which of the following statements is true?
o: Hal and Ivy are personally liable, because limited partners who take part in control of the business lose their shield.
Hal and Ivy are personally liable, because using a corporation as general partner is a sham designed to evade liability.
Hal and Ivy are not personally liable, because they acted only as officers of the corporate general partner.
Hal and Ivy are personally liable only up to the value of their shares in Westgate GP, Inc.
None of the above.
oe: Frigidaire held that the two did not take part in control as individuals; they acted as officers of the corporate general partner. And ULPA (2001) § 303 has since largely eliminated the control rule anyway.
Using a corporate general partner is a common, legitimate structure. Its purpose is to give everyone in the LP limited liability.

Correct. They acted only as officers of the corporate general partner, and the supplier knew it was dealing with the corporation. If the corporation is undercapitalized, the remedy is to pierce its veil, not to treat the limited partners as general partners.
Shareholders of the corporate general partner risk only what they put into it; no rule makes them liable up to that amount for the LP's debts.
C is correct.

questions.tag: De facto LLC; LLC by estoppel
questions.q: Brandt agrees to excavate a site for Larkspur Homes, signing first in his own name. A month later the parties replace that contract with an identical one naming Brandt's new company, Ironwood Excavating, LLC, which Brandt signs as owner after signing its articles in good faith. The state does not file the articles until weeks later. Larkspur deals only with Ironwood after that, and the work is defective. Under Duray Development v. Perrin, is Brandt personally liable on the second contract?
o: Yes, because an LLC does not exist until the state files its articles.
Yes, because he was a party to the first contract and remains bound by it.
Yes, because the de facto corporation doctrine never applies to LLCs.
No, but only if Larkspur knew the articles had not yet been filed.
No, because Ironwood was a de facto LLC and Larkspur dealt with it.
oe: That was the trial court's view in Duray Development; the court of appeals held that the de facto doctrine survives the statute's timing rule.
The first contract was superseded by the second, which named only the LLC, so it is not the basis of liability.
Duray Development applied both the de facto doctrine and corporation by estoppel to LLCs.
Estoppel does not depend on the third party's knowledge of the defect; it rests on Larkspur's having dealt with the business as an LLC.

Correct. Brandt acted in good faith under a valid statute for a lawful purpose and had executed articles, so Ironwood was a de facto LLC; and Larkspur, having dealt with Ironwood as an LLC, is estopped to deny its existence (Duray Development).
questions.e: A defectively formed LLC can still shield its owner: Michigan applies the de facto corporation doctrine (good faith, valid statute, lawful purpose, executed articles) and corporation by estoppel to LLCs (Duray Development).

questions.q: Under the RULLCA, the operating agreement of Ridge Coffee, LLC states that the company is "manager-managed" and names Sam as its manager. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Matters in the ordinary course of the company's activities are decided by the manager.
A majority of the members may remove Sam as manager at any time, without notice or cause.
Sam may amend the operating agreement on his own, because he controls the company's management.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. In a manager-managed LLC, matters relating to the company's activities and affairs are decided exclusively by the manager or managers, except as the act provides (§ 407(c)(1)).
True. A manager may be removed at any time by a majority of the members without notice or cause (§ 407(c)(4)).
False. Amending the operating agreement requires the consent of all members, even in a manager-managed LLC (§ 407(c)(3)).
Correct. The manager decides ordinary-course matters, and a majority of the members may remove the manager without cause. Acts outside the ordinary course and amendments still need all the members.
C is false; amendments need every member's consent.

questions.tag: Implied covenant can't override an express veto
questions.q: Arlo founded Pellucid Bio, LLC, a Delaware LLC; Wren's investment fund holds the other class of interests. The agreement requires 75% board approval for any financing, so neither side can act alone. Wren's representatives repeatedly vote down Arlo's financing plans, and the company runs out of cash. Arlo sues Wren's fund for breaching the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Under Fisk Ventures v. Segal, what is the most likely result?
o: Arlo loses, because exercising a veto the agreement grants is not a breach of the implied covenant.
Arlo wins, because members must support whatever financing is in the company's best interests.
Arlo loses, because Delaware LLC agreements may eliminate the implied covenant entirely.
Arlo wins, because blocking needed financing is arbitrary conduct that denies him the fruits of the bargain.
Arlo loses, but only because the fund made a counteroffer to provide some financing.
oe: Correct. Financing was expressly covered by the 75% requirement, which implied a right to disapprove, and the mere exercise of a contractual right is not a breach of the implied covenant (Fisk Ventures).
The agreement did not oblige one class to accept the other's business judgment, and the court refused to decide whose judgment was better.
The implied covenant is the one protection Delaware does not let LLC agreements eliminate (R & R Capital); Arlo loses for a different reason.
The implied covenant fills gaps; it cannot be used where the agreement expressly addresses the subject, and the 75% requirement gave each side a right to block.
The counteroffer was not the basis of the decision; the veto right itself defeated the claim.
questions.e: The implied covenant cannot be invoked where the agreement expressly covers the subject, and exercising a bargained-for veto is no breach (Fisk Ventures).

questions.tag: No piercing without injustice; clean hands
questions.q: Nadia forms Pinecrest Development, LLC to build a store for Glenmark Grocers and signs a 10-year lease to Glenmark as landlord, falsely saying she already owns the land. Glenmark ignores the lender's repeated requests for its financial statements; when they finally arrive, the lender refuses the loan because Glenmark's net worth is negative. The project dies, and Glenmark sues Nadia personally, asking the court to pierce Pinecrest's veil. Under Tom Thumb Food Markets v. TLH Properties, what is the most likely result?
o: Piercing is allowed, because Nadia misrepresented her ownership of the land.
Piercing is allowed, because a newly formed LLC with no assets is inherently a sham.
Piercing is denied, because LLC members can never be personally liable for an LLC's lease.
Piercing is denied, because the lease had a financing contingency that excused performance.
Piercing is denied, because there is no injustice and Glenmark caused its own loss.
oe: A misstatement is not enough; the court found no intent to mislead and no injustice from respecting the LLC.
Forming an LLC for a legitimate project is not a sham; Pinecrest was formed to build the store, not to defraud.
Veil piercing applies to LLCs (in Minnesota, by statute); it failed here on the facts, not because it is unavailable.
The court held the opposite: the lease had no contingency, so the LLC breached. Only the piercing ruling was reversed.

Correct. Piercing requires both alter-ego conduct and an injustice or fundamental unfairness. The LLC was formed for a legitimate purpose, and Glenmark lacked clean hands because its own delay and finances killed the financing (Tom Thumb Food Markets).
questions.e: Piercing an LLC requires (1) alter-ego conduct and (2) injustice or fundamental unfairness, and a plaintiff seeking that equitable remedy must have clean hands (Tom Thumb Food Markets).

questions.q: Members of Lakeside Football Club, LLC formed it to win a professional soccer franchise. Its operating agreement says members may engage in "any other business venture of any nature, including any venture which might be competitive with the business of the Company." When a stadium owner offers a lease, member Tamsin, purporting to act for the LLC without consulting the others, rejects it three times. Member Odell, who told the owner he would sign only if Tamsin would not, then signs in his own name and wins the franchise through a new firm. Under McConnell v. Hunt Sports Enterprises, did Odell breach a fiduciary duty?
o: No, because the agreement let members compete and he acted openly.
Yes, because he took an opportunity that the LLC was formed to pursue.
Yes, because members of an LLC owe each other a duty not to compete with the company.
No, because members of an LLC owe each other no fiduciary duties at all.
No, but only because Tamsin's group approved his signing the lease.
oe: Correct. The clause was unambiguous and permitted members to compete for the franchise; Odell used no company assets, acted openly, and stepped in only after Tamsin rejected the lease (McConnell).
Ordinarily that would be a breach, but the competition clause covered exactly this kind of competing venture.
That is the default rule, but McConnell held that an operating agreement may limit or define the scope of members' duties, and this one expressly allowed competition.
Members do owe each other the duty of utmost trust and loyalty; the agreement only narrowed its scope here.
Tamsin's group never approved the lease; Odell prevailed because of the clause and the open way he acted.
questions.e: An operating agreement may limit or define members' fiduciary duties, for example by permitting competition with the company, and conduct within that permission is no breach (McConnell).

questions.tag: Conflicted members may vote; duty to deal fairly
questions.q: Fern owns 50% of Dockside Storage, LLC, a Wisconsin LLC, and brothers Abel and Gus "collectively" own the other 50%. Abel and Fern, without telling Gus, vote to sell the LLC's warehouse at its original cost to a new company owned only by the two of them. Under Gottsacker v. Monnier, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: The vote is void, because Abel could not vote without his brother Gus.
The vote is void, because a member with a material conflict of interest may not vote.
The vote is valid, but they must not willfully fail to deal fairly with the LLC.
The vote is valid, and its fairness cannot be questioned because a majority approved it.
None of the above.
oe: That was the dissent's view. The majority read "collectively" as the sum of the brothers' individual 25% interests, so Abel could vote his own share.
The court held that the Wisconsin act does not bar a conflicted member from voting.

Correct. The majority held that a member with a material conflict may vote but must not willfully fail to deal fairly with the LLC or its members, and remanded for findings on fairness; the two must also account for any improper personal profit (Gottsacker).
Majority approval did not end the inquiry; the court sent the case back to decide whether the conflicted members dealt fairly.
C is correct.
questions.e: Under the Wisconsin act, a member with a material conflict of interest may vote but may not willfully fail to deal fairly with the LLC or its members (Gottsacker).

questions.q: When a member dissociates from an LLC under the RULLCA, what happens to the member's economic interest by default?
o: The LLC must buy it at fair value, as in a RUPA buyout.
The member keeps it only as a transferee.
The LLC dissolves so that the member can be paid.
The member forfeits it to the other members.
None of the above.
oe: The RULLCA has no mandatory buyout.
Correct (§ 603(a)(3)). Dissociation does not entitle the person to a distribution (§ 404(b)). This is a key difference from the RUPA § 701 buyout.
A member's dissociation does not dissolve the LLC.
Nothing is forfeited.
B is correct.

questions.tag: Waiving judicial dissolution: Delaware vs. RULLCA
questions.q: The members of an LLC agree in its operating agreement that "no member may seek a court decree of dissolution, and this Agreement is each member's sole entitlement on dissolution." Which of the following statements is true?
o: In Delaware the waiver is enforceable.
Under RULLCA the waiver cannot bar a member from seeking judicial dissolution.
In Delaware the waiver also eliminates the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. R & R Capital enforced a materially identical waiver: § 18-802 is not a mandatory provision, and Delaware's policy is freedom of contract.
True. A RULLCA operating agreement may not vary the judicial dissolution grounds of § 701(a)(4) (RULLCA § 105(c)(9)).
False. R & R Capital stressed that the implied covenant survives as an unwaivable protection; that is what makes the rest of the Act so flexible.
Correct. Delaware enforces the waiver (R & R Capital), while RULLCA forbids it (§ 105(c)(9)), and in neither does the waiver eliminate the implied covenant.
Incorrect, because C is false.
questions.e: Delaware members may waive the right to seek judicial dissolution, though the implied covenant remains (R & R Capital); RULLCA § 105(c)(9) forbids varying the judicial grounds.

questions.q: Under DLLCA § 18-802, as Fisk Ventures v. Segal described the case law, which of the following is NOT one of the circumstances courts look for in deciding that it is not reasonably practicable to carry on an LLC's business?
o: The members' vote is deadlocked at the board level.
The operating agreement gives no means of getting around the deadlock.
The company's finances leave effectively no business to operate.
One member holds an option to sell its interest to the company.
None of the above.
oe: One of the three circumstances.
One of the three circumstances.
One of the three circumstances.

Correct: not one of the circumstances. In Fisk Ventures the court held that a member's own put option is not an exit mechanism the company can use to break a deadlock, so its existence did not defeat dissolution.
D is not one of the circumstances.
questions.e: Delaware courts dissolve an LLC under § 18-802 when, weighed together, (1) the members are deadlocked, (2) the agreement gives no way around it, and (3) there is effectively no business to run; none is required or dispositive (Fisk Ventures).

questions.q: What principle does Rose v. Giamatti illustrate?
o: One can be an agent for some purposes but not others.
The Commissioner was MLB's agent for every purpose, because MLB appointed him.
Agency requires a written contract between principal and agent.
Arbitrators are always agents of the parties who appoint them.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The clubs had given the Commissioner exclusive, independent disciplinary authority they could not control, like an arbitrator, so he was not MLB's agent for discipline.
Appointment alone did not make him an agent for discipline.
No writing is required to create agency.
The court reasoned the opposite: independent authority is inconsistent with agency.
A is correct.

questions.tag: Members of an unincorporated association (Karl Rove)
questions.q: The Ridge Runners, an unincorporated hiking club, has no assets. At a meeting, members Ana and Ben vote to rent a mountain lodge for the club's retreat and direct the treasurer to sign the rental contract; member Cal votes no; member Dee is absent. The club cannot pay the $8,000 rent. Under Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh, who is personally liable to the lodge?
o: Every member of the club, because members of an unincorporated association are always liable for its debts.
Ana, Ben, and Cal, because each attended the meeting where the contract was approved.
Only the treasurer, because she signed the contract.
No one, because an association with no assets cannot enter a binding contract.
Ana and Ben, because they authorized the contract, and the treasurer signed it as their agent.
oe: Membership alone is not the test. A member is bound by contracts he authorized, assented to, or ratified.
Attending a meeting and voting no is not authorizing, assenting to, or ratifying the contract.
The treasurer may also be liable as a party, but Ana and Ben are bound because the treasurer acted as their agent.
Lack of assets does not void the contract; it means the lodge will look to those who authorized it.

Correct. A member of an unincorporated association is personally bound by contracts that he authorizes, assents to, or ratifies, personally or through an agent (Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh). Cal objected and Dee took no part.

questions.tag: Which route needs a change of position
questions.q: Under which theory does a principal's liability to a third party depend on the third party's detrimental change of position in reliance?
o: Estoppel.
Express actual authority.
Implied actual authority.
Ratification.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Estoppel requires the third party's justifiable, detrimental change of position, and it compensates the reliance loss (R3d § 2.05; Hoddeson).
Actual authority depends on the agent's understanding; the third party's reliance is irrelevant.
Also measured from the agent's perspective.
Ratification depends on the principal's later affirmance, not on the third party's reliance.
A is correct.

questions.q: The Restatement (Third) of Agency abandons inherent agency power. Under § 2.06, which of the following statements is true of an undisclosed principal?
o: It is liable to a third party who justifiably relies to its detriment on an unauthorized agent's conduct if the principal, on notice of that conduct, failed to take reasonable steps to notify the third party of the facts.
It may not rely on instructions that reduce the agent's authority below what the third party would assume if the principal were disclosed.
It is liable only if the third party knew the principal's identity.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: False. By definition, the third party does not know the undisclosed principal's identity.
Correct. These are the narrower, estoppel-like replacements for Watteau's rule.
C is wrong.

questions.q: Without authority, Ward signs a contract on behalf of his employer, Hollis Corp., to sell a used forklift to Kemp for $9,000. Kemp learns that Ward lacked authority and, before Hollis says anything, writes to Hollis withdrawing from the deal. Hollis then announces that it ratifies the sale. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Hollis's ratification binds Kemp, because ratification relates back to the moment Ward signed the contract.
Hollis's ratification binds Kemp, because a principal may ratify its agent's act at any time.
Hollis's ratification binds Kemp only if Hollis ratified in writing.
Hollis's ratification binds Kemp, because Kemp had no right to withdraw from a signed contract.
None of the above.
oe: Relation back does not apply once the third party has withdrawn. Ratification is not effective if it comes after the third party's manifestation of intent to withdraw (R3d § 4.05).
There are limits on timing: a third party's withdrawal before ratification, or a material change in circumstances, cuts off the power to ratify (§ 4.05).
The form of ratification is not the problem. Even a written ratification comes too late after Kemp withdrew.
Until Hollis ratified, there was no binding contract on Hollis's side, so Kemp was free to withdraw.
Correct. Ratification is not effective when, before it occurs, the third party has manifested its intent to withdraw (R3d § 4.05). Kemp withdrew first, so Hollis's later ratification cannot bind him.

questions.q: In Lind v. Schenley Industries, why was the company bound to Kaufman's promise of a 1% commission?
o: Kaufman had actual authority to set salesmen's pay.
Lind relied on Kaufman's own statements that he could set pay.
It held Kaufman out as Lind's boss on pay.
The company ratified the promise by paying commissions.
None of the above.
oe: Only the president could set pay; Kaufman lacked actual authority.
An agent's own statements cannot create apparent authority.
Correct. The vice president sent Lind to Kaufman about salary. The principal's manifestation through the position it gave Kaufman made Lind's belief reasonable.
The case rested on apparent (and inherent) authority, not ratification.
C is correct.

questions.q: A bank's loan officer, using the bank's letterhead and sitting in his bank office, persuades a customer to buy a "bank-guaranteed" certificate that does not exist and keeps the money. Under the Restatement (Third) of Agency, the bank's liability to the customer is best based on:
o: No theory, because fraud for one's own benefit is always outside the scope of employment.
Vicarious liability, because the officer committed the tort with apparent authority.
Negligent supervision only.
Ratification, which is required before a principal is liable for an agent's fraud.
None of the above.
oe: Scope of employment is not the only route. A tort committed with apparent authority makes the principal liable even if the agent served only himself.

Correct. R3d § 7.08: a principal is vicariously liable for an agent's tort when actions taken by the agent with apparent authority constitute the tort, as with fraud or misrepresentation that the third party believes is the principal's own dealing.
Direct liability for negligent supervision is possible if facts show it, but it is not needed when the agent acted with apparent authority.
Ratification is one basis for liability, not a prerequisite.
B is correct.

questions.q: On the last day before the statute of limitations runs, attorney Nash hires a courier service to file a client's complaint. The courier arrives after the clerk's office closes, and the claim is lost. The client sues Nash, who argues that the courier was an independent contractor. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Nash is not liable, because a principal is never liable for the negligence of an independent contractor.
Nash may be liable, because his duty to the client is nondelegable.
